hints: Look at where each part is on a mitotic chromosome: which one holds the middle together, which one is a whole copy, and which one caps the ends?

Recall what each part is made of: centromere is non-coding DNA in the middle, a chromatid is double-stranded DNA packaged with histones, and telomeres are protective repeated base sequences at the tips.
walkthrough:
**Start with the centromere in the middle**

Think of a mitotic chromosome as an X shape. The centromere is the pinched region of non-coding DNA that holds the two sister chromatids together until anaphase.

It definitely contains DNA, so any option saying no DNA is wrong.

**Check what a chromatid really is**

Each chromatid is one complete copy made during interphase. It is a double-stranded DNA molecule coiled around histone proteins to form nucleosomes.

So it is not a single polynucleotide, it is a double helix plus histones.

**Finish with the telomere at the tips**

Telomeres cap and protect the ends of each chromatid. They are made of many short repeated sequences of bases that are non-coding.

They do not hold chromatids together and they are not defined by many C and G bases.

**Put it all together**

Only row B gives all three correctly: centromere holds two chromatids together, chromatid is double-stranded DNA with histones, telomere is repeated sequences. Well done, that is your match.

options.A: Incorrect because the centromere contains DNA, a chromatid is double-stranded DNA not a single polynucleotide, and telomeres are short repeated sequences not a C and G rich region.
options.B: Correct because the centromere is non-coding DNA holding chromatids together, a chromatid is double-stranded DNA with histones, and the telomere is repeated base sequences protecting the ends.
options.C: Incorrect because the centromere description is wrong and the telomere description is mixed up. The protective end cap is the telomere, not the centromere.
options.D: Incorrect because it swaps roles. The centromere holds chromatids together until anaphase (not prophase), while telomeres protect ends, they do not hold ends together.
